I will keep my full 20 mu in the wheat-maize rotation, because that is the system I know best, it fits Quzhou County conditions, and I have well irrigation so I can support both crops at the key stages. For wheat, I will use improved seed rather than old traditional seed, because I want stable emergence, better lodging resistance, and more reliable yield. I will not push fertilizer to extremes; I will use a moderate, steady rate of nitrogen with enough phosphorus and some potassium, because after many years of farming I care more about dependable output than gambling on very high input. I will irrigate wheat three times if water conditions stay normal: once after sowing or at wintering if needed, once at jointing, and once around grain filling, because those are the stages that matter most for my yield. I will use rotary tillage for wheat after maize residue management, because it is practical for my scale and labor situation. I will spray pesticides twice for wheat, mainly to control diseases, aphids, and weeds when pressure appears, because clean fields and healthy leaves matter.

For summer maize, I will also plant the full 20 mu right after wheat harvest, and I will use hybrid seed, because for maize I trust hybrids more for vigor and yield. I will keep fertilizer balanced but put a bit more nitrogen on maize than on wheat, since maize responds strongly if the stand is good and rain plus irrigation match well. I will irrigate maize twice in a normal year, mainly around seedling establishment if moisture is short and again near tasseling-silking, because that is when drought hurts most. I will keep rotary tillage here too, because it lets me turn the season around quickly after wheat harvest. I will spray pesticides twice for maize, mainly for weeds and insect pressure, because I do not want avoidable losses. My decisions are based on what I can manage steadily with my experience, my family labor situation, my land size, and my irrigation access.
